overview: Here Scots means early Gaelic-speaking western communities associated with Dál Riata and its successors, rather than all modern Scottish people or speakers of the later Scots language. Dunadd and island monasteries reveal craft, food, learning and sea connections.

periods.title: Earlier Dál Riata
periods.summary: Dunadd was a royal and craft centre. Its sixth- to eighth-century remains provide background to the map label.

periods.title: Changing western communities
periods.summary: Rulers and island connections changed during this interval; it is not one independent kingdom’s secure lifespan.

items.text: Excavations at Dunadd found moulds and debris from a seventh-century workshop making fine metalwork. Brooch production involved planning, heating and finishing. This earlier evidence shows the skills behind the ornaments worn by powerful households.

Some Dunadd brooch designs adapted Anglo-Saxon forms. Imported pottery and glass also reached this Argyll hillfort. Objects crossed political and language boundaries; a foreign-looking ornament does not by itself identify its wearer's birthplace.

The early excavations recovered 54 stone querns used to grind grain. Feeding a gathering required repeated physical work before anyone sat down to a feast. A royal meeting also needed someone to make the flour.

Dál Riata contained several kindreds with their own territories. Scholars have suggested that Dunadd offered a meeting place between them. The footprint carved near its summit is interpreted as an inauguration feature, not a surviving royal footprint pressed into wet rock.

Iona was connected to Ireland and mainland Scotland by boat. Its island position could help communication rather than simply isolate its community. The standing thirteenth-century abbey is much later than Columba's sixth-century foundation.

Adomnán's Life of Columba, written before 704, mentions fishing nets, deer traps and salt stores. This earlier monastic account gives specific glimpses of obtaining and preserving food; it is also a saint's biography with a religious purpose.

The same account mentions harvest labour, book satchels and ink horns. Monastic learning depended on farming and supplies as well as prayer. A beautifully written page had a working community behind it.

At Inchmarnock, excavators recovered slates carrying trial letters, designs and scraps of text. Some are interpreted as pupils' work. Reusable stone offered a surface for practice before committing writing to costly parchment.

The Inchmarnock collection includes Latin and Gaelic writing, with ogham examples dated broadly to the seventh-ninth centuries. Other slates are much later. Finding several scripts together does not make every inscription contemporary.

sections.title: A small book with several lives

items.text: The Book of Deer is a small parchment Gospel book, about 16 by 11 centimetres. Cambridge's catalogue dates its main production to the late 800s or early 900s and cautiously suggests Scotland. Its compact size contrasts with the labour of preparing skin, copying and painting.

The book contains a service for visiting the sick alongside Gospel texts. This is evidence of religious care, not proof of an effective medical treatment. Gaelic notes about Deer's property were added in the 1100s, well after the main book.

In principio, “In the beginning,” appears at the opening of John on folio 42r of the Book of Deer. It is Latin written in an Insular manuscript, not a sample of everyday Gaelic speech. The short phrase introduces a sacred text.

ending.text: Dál Riata’s political world changed, but Gaelic-speaking communities continued through later kingdoms and island societies. The map changes labels at 1000; that is not an extinction date or proof of an unbroken independent western state.
